content: 1. A total of 27 studies met the inclusion criteria for targeted client communication (TCC) via mobile phones for sexual and reproductive health among adults. Of these, 8 studies were conducted in high-income countries, 8 in upper-middle-income countries, 9 in lower-middle-income countries, 1 in a low-income country, and 1 trial was conducted across two countries (South Africa, an upper-middle-income country, and Uganda, a low-income country). 2. For TCC via mobile phones targeting adolescents, 13 studies met the inclusion criteria. Except for one trial conducted in a lower-middle-income country (Ghana), all other trials were conducted in high-income countries. 3. Regarding TCC for pregnant and postpartum women, 11 studies met the inclusion criteria. Among these, 4 were conducted in high-income countries, 2 in upper-middle-income countries, 4 in lower-middle-income countries, and 1 in a low-income country. 4. For TCC targeting pregnant and postpartum women living with HIV, 3 studies met the inclusion criteria. All of these studies were conducted in Kenya, a lower-middle-income country. 5. For TCC targeting parents and caregivers of children under 5 years of age, 14 studies met the inclusion criteria. Of these, 6 were conducted in high-income countries, 7 in lower-middle-income countries, and 1 in a low-income country. 6. A summary of findings table is available for the results of the review, including a plain language summary. For digital TCC targeting adolescents compared to standard care in primary healthcare settings, the population studied included adolescents aged 14–24 years in community settings in high-income countries (e.g., Australia and the USA). The intervention involved reminders and/or information/education delivered via SMS and/or voice calls, compared to standard care or no intervention. 7. The certainty of evidence for the effect of the intervention on clinic attendance for STI testing among adolescents was assessed as very low. This was based on one randomized controlled trial (RCT) conducted in Australia, with no studies reporting on the timeliness of information and services. 8. The effect of the intervention on condom use among adolescents was also assessed as very low certainty, based on one RCT conducted in Australia. Similarly, the effect on contraception use at 6 months among adolescents was assessed as low certainty, based on one RCT conducted in the USA. 9. The effect of the intervention on adherence to antiretroviral medication among adolescents was assessed as very low certainty, based on two RCTs conducted in the USA. The effect on HIV treatment success (measured by viral load suppression) among previously non-adherent adolescents was also assessed as very low certainty. 10. Client satisfaction and acceptability of the intervention were reported in two studies. One study found that over 90% of participants were satisfied with the number, content, and length of messages received. However, another study reported that 24% of participants found SMS messages annoying at 12 months. 11. The effect of the intervention on knowledge and attitudes about sexual health and STIs among adolescents was assessed as very low certainty, with no studies reporting on providers' acceptability or satisfaction with the intervention. 12. No studies were identified that reported on the effect of the intervention on resource use or unintended consequences. One study reported a 6% cost increase associated with the intervention, but the certainty of this evidence was assessed as very low. 13. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines viral failure as a persistently detectable viral load exceeding 1000 copies/mL (based on two consecutive viral load measurements within a 3-month interval with adherence support) after at least 6 months of antiretroviral therapy (ART). Treatment success is defined as two consecutive viral load measurements below 1000 copies/mL. 14. The GRADE Working Group grades of evidence were used to assess the certainty of evidence. High certainty indicates confidence that the true effect is close to the estimate, while very low certainty indicates little confidence in the effect estimate, with the true effect likely to differ substantially.
